sentences.text: Last time we built Alder's pile coin by coin, and read its p-value from the tail: 3.5%.
Exact, and a fair amount of work.
In practice, people often skip the pile. Three shortcuts are in everyday use: a bell curve, a ruler, and brute-force flipping.
Each gives Alder a p-value of its own. Will all three land on the same side of 5%? And is there a clinic where a shortcut goes badly wrong?
Welcome back to Model in Motion.
Today: three shortcuts.
The first shortcut replaces the pile with a bell curve of the same centre and the same spread.
For Alder, that is centred on 8.02, with a standard deviation of 2.22.
Alder's 13 is 4.98 above the centre. Divide by the spread: 2.24 standard deviations out.
The bell curve's two tails beyond that hold 2.5%.
That is the score test. It needs just three numbers: observed, expected, and the spread.
It is our old friend, observed minus expected, measured in standard units.
The second shortcut never looks at the count. It goes back to the sliders.
Alder's gamma sits 0.87 above the reference, and Episode 9 gave it a standard error of 0.43.
0.87 over 0.43 is 2.02 standard errors, and a p-value of 4.4%. That is the Wald test.
The third shortcut takes last episode's opening idea seriously. Flip Alder's thirty coins ten thousand times, and simply count.
This run gives a p-value of 3.8%.
It homes in on the exact pile as the rounds add up. But with ten thousand rounds, it cannot report anything rarer than one in ten thousand.
The software calls this one a bootstrap.
So, Alder four ways: 3.5% exact, 2.5% by the bell curve, 4.4% by the ruler, 3.8% by flipping.
All below 5%. All four flag Alder, and none of the tests flags anyone else.
But look at Elm. Exact and bell curve agree: about one and a half standard units below the reference.
The ruler says only 0.7. It is measuring from a gamma that does not exist.
That is the ruler's first weakness. Its second is one we have met: which standard error?
Record the risk factor sixty-five units higher, as an age in years might be, and the textbook standard error of Alder's gamma becomes 38. The test collapses to 0.02.
Taken at the average case mix, it stays at 2.02.
The bell curve's weakness is small numbers. Elm expects fewer than two readmissions, and a bell curve centred there spills below zero.
In our crowds where every provider equals the reference, among those with fewer than fifty patients, the exact test flags 4.7%, the bell curve 4.9%, and the ruler only 4.0%.
Each test also turns inside out into an interval. For Alder's ratio: 1.04 to 2.26, exact. 1.07 to 2.25 by the bell curve. 1.02 to 2.31 by the ruler.
So which one, when? The exact test for flags: it is the software's default.
The bell curve when you need a formula. It costs almost nothing, and next time it will draw smooth limits.
The ruler for anything built on gamma itself. And flipping, as a check on the others.
Let's gather it up.
The bell curve swaps the pile for a normal curve with the same centre and spread.
The ruler measures the gap between sliders in standard errors.
Flipping rebuilds the pile by brute force. On Alder, all three agree with the exact test. On small clinics, they can part ways.
We now have a verdict for every clinic. Five verdicts are easy to read. What about two hundred, or seven thousand?
Next time: the funnel.
This has been Model in Motion. Thanks for following the story.
